report:
(Fictional case study for training. Not a real investigation.)

What happened

MV Tarrakin Star, a 24.4 m aluminium catamaran passenger ferry certificated for 96 passengers, departed Muntari Island at 17:35:02 on 7 July 2026 on service TF18 to Kanooka Heads. Times in this report are local time (UTC+10). The vessel carried 38 passengers, a master, a deckhand and a kiosk attendant. Sunset was at 17:02 and civil twilight ended at 17:29, so the channel transit was made in darkness, as the 31st darkness transit of the service since the winter timetable began on 1 June 2026. The water was flat, the wind was 305 to 310 degrees at 8 to 9 kt, visibility was over 10 km, the moon was 2% illuminated, and there was no other traffic. The tide was falling, and the gauge read 0.91 m at 18:12.

The vessel entered the Merrandi Channel at 18:03:58 and was 1 m west of the charted centreline abeam the No. 2 beacon at 18:05:30, at 8.4 kt on course 195 degrees. The deckhand had been sent to collect fares at 18:04:14, so no one else was on the bridge with the master. At 18:07:06 the chart plotter display (the screen showing the vessel's position on the chart) froze, with cause code 0x51, and did not recover. The heading began to ease from 195 to 200 degrees in the same second. The master said that the heading was eased five degrees while attending to the plotter and then looking for the beacon, and that they never made a decision to turn. The master did not slow or stop the vessel. It is virtually certain that this heading change took the vessel out of the dredged channel on the bank side, because the recorded rate of turn, rudder angle and absence of any cross-set show a heading applied and held rather than a current or wind effect.

With the plotter frozen, the master looked for the No. 4 beacon by eye. The master said "Right. Where's four" at 18:08:31, when the vessel was 0.47 nm north of the beacon, and "There's four" at 18:10:02, 91 seconds later, when it was 0.25 nm north. The vessel crossed the western edge of the dredged channel at about 18:09:00, was 39 m west of the centreline at 18:10:02, and was over Boolarong Bank from about 18:11:00. The master said the beacon was then dead ahead, and that they eased the vessel back to port, believing it was just outside the channel edge. The course over ground came back only from 200 to 197 degrees, still west of the channel's 195 degrees. The shallow alarm sounded at 18:11:48, set at 0.9 m under the keel, the value written into the setup in 2019. Both throttles went astern at 18:11:52, and the vessel made contact with Boolarong Bank at 18:12:04 at 6.8 kt. It stopped within 11 m, heeled 4 degrees to starboard, 74 m west of the charted centreline and 54 m outside the dredged channel.

The starboard hull bottom plating was set up over 4.1 m with a 180 mm split in way of the No. 2 void (a watertight compartment in the hull), and ingress had reached approximately 260 mm by the time the vessel refloated. The starboard propeller blades were bent, the shaft was bent 1.4 mm, the rudder stock was distorted 3 degrees and the starboard skeg was torn away. There were no serious injuries. One passenger reported a grazed shin and two were treated at the wharf for distress. The master stopped both engines at 18:12:31 and did not restart them. At 18:13:04 the master broadcast a pan pan (an urgent radio message) stating that the vessel was not attempting to refloat. The master's reasoning in interview was a falling tide, an unknown bottom and 38 people aboard, and that a vessel cannot sink while on the bank. Backing a holed vessel off into deeper water on a falling tide was therefore never attempted. Lifejackets were issued, with all 38 passengers in them by about 18:22. The port workboat came alongside at 18:41 and the last passenger was ashore at 19:26. The vessel refloated on the tide at 00:20 and was withdrawn from service, and the Merrandi Channel was closed to commercial traffic for 19 hours. [NOT ESTABLISHED: cost of damage or repair status of the vessel]

Why it happened

The grounding followed from the loss of the chart plotter, an unnoticed heading change and a transit that continued at eight knots without a means of fixing the vessel's position. Organisational and equipment conditions shaped each step.

The loss of the plotter and the transit that continued

The plotter's internal event log recorded the display process not responding at 18:07:06 with no reset, and the bridge audio matched it to the second, with "Oh, come on" at 18:07:11 and "(unintelligible) frozen again" at 18:07:44. The same cause code, 0x51, had been logged at 10:42 and 11:17 that morning, when the unit recovered itself. A 46 hour bench test on 21/07/2026 did not reproduce the fault and found no defect, so the physical cause of the freeze could not be determined. The approved electronics contractor did find that code 0x51 was known to the manufacturer and addressed by firmware issued in 11/2024, which had never been applied to this unit. It is extremely likely that the freeze removed the primary means of position fixing the passage plan named, and that the master then made the rest of the transit without it.

The firmware fix did not reach the unit because the operator's defect procedure did not make a self-clearing fault visible. OPS-9 9.1 required immediate reporting only of a defect that made the vessel unseaworthy or affected a statutory item. Paragraph 9.2 put all other defects in the defect book at the end of the shift in which they were found, and 9.3 required the outgoing master to brief the relieving master on any defect without requiring that the brief be written down. The plotter was not a statutory item on this vessel on this route, although the passage plan named it as the primary means of fixing. The manual did not say whether a fault that had come and gone was a defect. Both masters read it the same way, and the master put it as "The book is for things that are broken when you hand over. If it's broken you write it, if it came good you say it." The book's eleven entries in the 90 days before the occurrence were all faults present when written, and none concerned the plotter. The outgoing master said the plotter had frozen three or four times on this vessel in the previous year and that none was written up. The relieving master said it had frozen on them a month earlier, and it froze twice on the morning of 07/07/2026. The maintenance system held no work order, fault report or correspondence about the plotter in 2026, and the operator held no subscription to the manufacturer's bulletins. The procedure likely allowed the fault to remain unrectified, because recorded freezes would have reached the Operations Manager's weekly review and the maintenance system, and from there the contractor, who needed one bench test to name the fix. Against this, a recorded freeze might have been reviewed at the end of the week, noted and left, because nobody ashore held the bulletin. [NOT ESTABLISHED: how many recorded freezes it would have taken to send the unit to the contractor]

The freeze would not necessarily have led to a grounding had the master stopped. OPS-3 3.4 required the transit to be made on the centreline, monitored on the plotter, with the No. 2 and No. 4 beacons identified. Paragraph 3.6 required a reduction of speed and consideration of anchoring only in reduced visibility, which this was not. Appendix A, issue 2 and current, named the plotter as the primary means and the visual transit of the No. 4 beacon with the town wharf leading lights as the secondary. It stated that the plan was written for the daylight transit and that "Night transits are not scheduled on this route." It gave no guidance on loss of the plotter and named no abort or hold point. The leading lights were about 1.9 nm beyond the No. 6 beacon and did not resolve as two lights until the vessel was inside the channel's southern third, so at the point of the freeze the beacon was the whole of the secondary means. The outgoing master said they would have "taken the way off her and sat there", and added that no rule they knew of required it. The master said nothing in any document asks the question. The AIS track recorded no reduction of speed after the freeze, with 8.4 kt at the freeze and 8.1 kt at 18:08:00. The vessel crossed the channel's western edge 114 seconds after the freeze. It could have been stopped in 92 m, there was no other traffic, the water was flat, and a stop begun before about 18:11:40 would have left it short of the contact point. The master said stopping was not considered, and that they went to the visual transit because in their mind it was the backup. It is very likely that the absence of a night passage plan and hold point allowed the transit to continue at speed, and it is extremely likely that the continued transit itself turned the loss of the plotter into a grounding. The same continued transit left the vessel only 16 seconds' warning from the shallow alarm, as set out below. The master's decision at 18:10:02 not to stop after seeing the beacon dead ahead, because the master took the vessel to be just outside the edge when it was 39 m west of the centreline, belongs to the same pattern. The operator recorded that a hold point cost nothing on that night, and the investigator found that both masters interviewed said stopping was the right answer. Although a master who did not think of stopping unprompted might not have applied a written rule under the same pressure, a named hold point would have applied throughout the 114 seconds.

Why the transit was in darkness without a plan

RRA-07 issue 2 (03/2023) was the current route risk assessment. It carried the restriction "daylight transits only" and stated that a night transit required the General Manager Operations' approval and a specific passage plan. CHG-2026-014, approved by the Operations Manager on 22/04/2026, moved TF18 from 16:15 to 17:35 from 01/06/2026, assessed the change as "timetable change only", recorded "no new hazard identified" and answered "No" to route risk assessment review. RRA-07 was not reopened, no issue 3 exists, no night passage plan was written, and the General Manager Operations' approval was neither sought nor given. TF18 then ran 31 times in darkness before the occurrence, which was the thirty-first. The master said the change brought a new roster sheet and nothing else. This process asked whether the change was new rather than whether the assessment still held. A review of RRA-07 against a night operation would have reached the unlit reach between the No. 2 and No. 4 beacons, which the assessment already named as a hazard, and could not have closed without a night plan. It is likely that moving the service into darkness without reopening the assessment led to there being no night plan or hold point. A reopened assessment might have produced a plan that said no more than the daylight one, so how good the plan would have been is open. Why the change was assessed as a timetable change only is [NOT ESTABLISHED: why the change was assessed as a timetable change only; the Operations Manager's account has been given verbally and has not been taken as a formal interview].

The beacon and the unnoticed heading change

From 18:07:06, the second the plotter froze, the heading increased from 195 to 200 degrees over about a minute and was then held. The rate of turn peaked at 6 degrees per minute at 18:07:40, and the rudder followed helm demand within 1.5 degrees, so the turn was steered. The wind was offshore at 8 kt and there was no cross-set at that state of tide. The master said, "I eased her to starboard while I was fiddling with the plotter and then looking for four. Five degrees. I never made that decision." The heading change was virtually certain to be the cause of the vessel leaving the dredged channel, which it did at about 18:09:00, 0.40 nm north of the No. 4 beacon, moving west at about 20 m a minute. The vessel was over Boolarong Bank from about 18:11:00.

Nothing on the bridge showed the new heading, because the plotter's vessel symbol was frozen and the No. 4 beacon was screened. A range and visibility check on 18/07/2026 from the port workboat found the beacon was not visible from the channel between 0.84 nm and 0.34 nm north of it. The sightline passed through the mangrove canopy on Merrandi Islet, 240 m up-channel of the beacon, which measured 5.8 m against a lantern height of 4.2 m. The master began looking at 18:08:31 when 0.47 nm north of the beacon and called it at 18:10:02 at 0.25 nm, 91 seconds later. Seen on the starboard bow where it belongs, the light would have shown the vessel drawing west while it was still in the channel. It is likely that the screening allowed the held heading to go unnoticed. The heading change began before the search, so the screening explains the turn going unnoticed and not the turn itself. The light was also clear of the islet for at least the last 37 seconds of the search, from about 18:09:25, and it was not seen in that time.

The screening was recorded long before the occurrence. Work order WO-118, raised 09/2023, recorded the regrowth, recommended trimming to 2 m on a three-yearly cycle and estimated $18,500. It was deferred at the 2023, 2024 and 2025 works rounds, each time "defer, unfunded, refer next round". WO-176, raised 03/2026, recorded the sightline as "now fully closed on the northern approach". The Authority's file note recorded that the islet was 240 m from the beacon and so fell outside the 50 m scope of schedule 2.4, and that the work therefore competed in the general waterways vote rather than the aids to navigation vote. The monthly check was made from the town wharf, 2.1 nm south of the beacon, where the islet is not in the line of sight, and recorded the beacon as "observed, operating" every month from 01/2024 to 07/2026. The canopy had grown from 2.1 m in 2019 at about half a metre a year, so a trim funded in 2023 would have left it near 3.5 m on the night, below the lantern. It is very likely that the deferral led to the screening, although the growth may not have been even over the seven years, since only two measurements exist. Neither master had reported the beacon in two years, because, in the outgoing master's words, "There's no form."

The shallow alarm

The echo sounder's shallow alarm was set to 0.9 m under the keel, the value written at commissioning in 2019 and never changed. It sounded at 18:11:48, both throttles went astern 4 seconds later, and contact followed at 18:12:04, 16 seconds after the alarm. At 7.1 kt the vessel covered 58 m in that time against its trials figure of 92 m for a crash stop from 8 kt. The alarm did what it was set to do. On the surveyed gradient of about 1 in 70 the alarm could not have sounded appreciably earlier at that setting, so the setting was extremely likely to have given too little warning to prevent contact once the vessel was over the bank. The contact was at 6.8 kt, and the vessel stopped within 11 m.

Matters examined that could not be settled

The investigation examined whether the boat ramp floodlights delayed the sighting of the beacon, and the matter is still being examined. The survey on 18/07/2026 found 14 unshielded LED floodlights on 12 m columns at the new boat ramp, each presenting about 4,800 candela toward the channel, commissioned on 22/05/2026. From 0.5 nm north of the beacon the array lay behind it within 4 degrees of bearing and 1.5 degrees of elevation, and was continuously lit while the beacon flashed green for 0.4 seconds every 2.5 seconds. The master described looking "into a wall of light", and the outgoing master called the beacon "washed out altogether from up the top". Against that, the beacon was screened over most of the search and would not have been visible against a black background either, and the heading change began before the search, so the floodlights cannot have caused the turn. The Port Authority's aids to navigation officer was not consulted on the development. No measurement exists of what could be seen on the night, only a survey eleven days later, and the master said twice that they could not tell whether the lights were why they could not see the beacon. Whether the floodlights delayed the sighting is about as likely as not on the evidence available. What would resolve it is [NOT ESTABLISHED: a measured detection threshold for a 0.4 second green flash against that background].

Whether the master was fatigued during the transit also could not be settled. The master was on day nine of a twelve-day tour, on a split duty of 05:40 to 08:40 and 13:00 to 19:20 with a 13 hour 40 minute spread, and had 6 hours 15 minutes of sleep. The master said, "I was tired. I'd be lying if I said otherwise." Against this, the master said "I wasn't fighting to stay awake and I wasn't slow", and the recorded performance agreed. Helm work held the centreline to within 3 m for the first two minutes in the channel, the response to the shallow alarm took 4 seconds, and the radio work after the grounding was correct at the first attempt. The decision not to refloat was made in about thirty seconds and was right. Whether the master was fatigued is about as likely as not. No detailed fatigue assessment was made, because every decision that mattered was either answered by another factor or contradicted by the recorded data, so established fatigue would still not have been found to contribute on this evidence.

Considered and not found contributing

A tide set down below prediction was very unlikely. The Port Authority gauge read 0.91 m at 18:12 against a predicted 0.94 m, and the gauge's largest departure from the table in the twelve hours to 20:00 was 0.07 m. At the predicted height the vessel would have touched as well, because it was 54 m outside a channel dredged to 3.2 m.

A steering or propulsion failure before the vessel left the centreline was very unlikely. The engines held within 12 rpm of each other with no alarm, steering hydraulic pressure held at 96 to 99 bar, and rudder angle followed helm demand within 1.5 degrees. The whole steering system was removed and tested on 12/07/2026 and every component was serviceable.

The plotter fault passed on verbally at the 13:05 change of master and not entered in the defect book was found not to contribute, because it was unlikely to have changed the outcome. Both masters made the same omission and both volunteered it, so it is an instance of the procedure gap described above. An entry at 13:05 would have been reviewed by the Operations Manager at the end of the week, and nothing written that afternoon could have applied firmware to the unit or taken the vessel off TF18 by 18:07.

Other risks that did not contribute

Several further conditions increased risk but were found not to have contributed. The solar conversion of the No. 4 beacon in 11/2025 halved its nominal range from 6 nautical miles to 3, with a measured 2.6 nm. It was unlikely to have contributed, because the beacon was screened over the half mile in which the vessel left the channel, the master already knew the light was weaker, and the search ran well inside the measured range. No notice reached any user of the channel, and the passage plan still recorded the beacon at 6 M. WAN-2 section 4.2 applied availability and notification duties only to declared shipping channels, and the Merrandi Channel was not one. This was unlikely to have contributed, because a notice of the range change or an availability figure would not have made a screened light visible. The winter roster closed a split duty within 20 minutes of the operator's 14 hour spread limit on every day of the tour. This was unlikely to have contributed, because its only path to the occurrence ran through fatigue, and whether the master was fatigued is about as likely as not.

The forward saloon lifejacket locker, behind a kiosk counter fitted in a 2019 refit under a minor modification notice that did not trigger a re-survey, did not affect the grounding. It remains under examination as a matter of risk. The survey on 16/07/2026 found the locker face could not be reached from 22 of the 34 forward saloon seats without passing behind the counter through a 0.6 m gap, and the operator says the same counter is fitted to its two other 24 m vessels.

What we found

This section sets out what the investigation found, in the order of the sequence that led to the grounding of MV Tarrakin Star on Boolarong Bank, and then the matters that raised risk without contributing, the matters left unresolved and what worked. All times are local time (UTC+10).

Contributing safety factors

The factors below link in sequence. Organisational and procedural conditions allowed a frozen chart plotter (the vessel's screen display of its position) to go unanswered, and the master's unnoticed heading change then took the vessel out of the channel.

  • The chart plotter display froze at 18:07:06, 114 seconds before the vessel crossed the western edge of the channel. It did not recover. The unit's event log, the bridge audio and the master's account agree on the time. The freeze very probably contributed, in the sense that it was extremely likely, because everything that followed was done without the primary means of position fixing named in the passage plan.
  • The heading eased from 195 to 200 degrees over about a minute from the second of the freeze, while the master was at the frozen screen, and was then held. The master said in interview that the change was never a decision. The change contributed to the occurrence. With no current and no wind effect at that state of tide, it moved the vessel west at about 20 m a minute.
  • The vessel left the dredged channel on the bank side at about 18:09:00, 0.40 nm north of the No. 4 beacon. It was over Boolarong Bank from about 18:11:00. This contributed to the occurrence, because the grounding followed directly from the vessel being outside the channel.
  • The transit continued at eight knots from the freeze until the shallow alarm, with no reduction of speed and no consideration of stopping. The vessel could have been stopped in 92 m, there was no other traffic and the water was flat. A stop begun before about 18:11:40 would have left the vessel short of the contact point. This was extremely likely to have contributed. The master said that the visual transit was in mind as the backup, and that stopping on the edge of a bank that could not be seen felt worse than easing back in.
  • The shallow alarm was set at 0.9 m under the keel, the value written in at commissioning in 2019. It sounded at 18:11:48 and gave 16 seconds' warning. The vessel covered 58 m in that time against a crash stop distance of 92 m. The alarm did what it was set to do, but the setting was extremely likely to have contributed because it could not give enough time to stop.
  • The No. 4 beacon was screened by the mangrove canopy on Merrandi Islet from the channel between 0.84 nm and 0.34 nm north of it. The canopy measured 5.8 m against a lantern height of 4.2 m. With the plotter frozen, the beacon was the only means of fixing left. It was probably a contributing factor because it hid the one reference that would have shown the held heading. The master began looking at 18:08:31 and called the beacon at 18:10:02. The heading change itself began before the search, so the screening explains why the change went unnoticed and not why it began.
  • There was no night passage plan for the Merrandi Channel and no hold point for the loss of the primary means of position fixing. OPS-3 3.6 requires a speed reduction and consideration of anchoring, but only in reduced visibility, which this was not. The passage plan states that night transits are not scheduled. This was very likely a contributing factor. Both masters interviewed said that stopping was the right answer and that nothing in any document asks for it. (Safety issue)
  • OPS-9 never requires a fault that cleared itself to be recorded. Section 9.1 applies to a defect that makes the vessel unseaworthy or affects a statutory item, and the plotter is not a statutory item on this route. Section 9.2 requires an entry at the end of the shift in which a defect is found. The outgoing master believed the plotter had frozen three or four times on this vessel in the year before, and none was written down. The contractor identified cause code 0x51 as addressed by firmware issued in 11/2024, which this unit never received. The procedure was probably a contributing factor. A recorded freeze might still have been reviewed and left, because the operator held no subscription to the manufacturer's bulletins. (Safety issue)
  • The last service, TF18, was moved into darkness without reopening the daylight-only risk assessment. RRA-07 issue 2 restricts the channel to daylight transits and requires the General Manager Operations' approval and a specific passage plan for a night transit. CHG-2026-014, approved by the Operations Manager on 22/04/2026, assessed the change as a timetable change only and answered "No" to route risk assessment review. The service then ran 31 times in darkness, and the occurrence was the thirty-first. This was probably a contributing factor. A review would have required a night passage plan, although a plan might have said no more than the daylight one. (Safety issue)
  • Clearing of the beacon's sightline was deferred, unfunded, at the 2023, 2024 and 2025 works rounds. Work order WO-118 recommended trimming to 2 m at an estimated $18,500. The islet is 240 m from the beacon and so falls outside the 50 m vegetation scope of schedule 2.4 of the services agreement, which put the work in the general waterways vote. The canopy grew from 2.1 m in 2019 to 5.8 m in 07/2026. A trim funded in 2023 would have left it near 3.5 m, under the lantern. The deferral was very likely a contributing factor. (Safety issue)

Other factors that increased risk

These conditions were real and are worth acting on, but each was unlikely to have influenced this occurrence.

  • WAN-2 section 4.2 applies an availability target, a duty to record availability and a duty to give notice to mariners of a change of range, but only on a declared shipping channel. The Merrandi Channel is not one, so section 4.3 applies, and it requires only that the authority can show an inspection interval it set itself. This was unlikely to have influenced the occurrence, because a notice or an availability figure would not have made a screened light visible. It remains important because no user of the channel is owed any information about its aids. (Safety issue)
  • The No. 4 beacon was converted to a solar lantern in 11/2025. Its nominal range fell from 6 nm to 3 nm, and the investigator measured 2.6 nm on 18/07/2026. The hydrographic service was notified on 04/02/2026, and the chart correction was still pending on 07/07/2026. No local notice was issued, and the operator's passage plan still gave 6 M. This was unlikely to have influenced the occurrence, because the search ran from 0.47 nm to 0.25 nm, well inside the measured range, and the master already knew the light was weaker. Local notice LNM-2026-14 was issued on 22/07/2026, and Tarrakin Ferries reissued the passage plan appendix as issue 3 with the corrected range. (Safety issue)
  • The roster put the darkness transit at the end of a split duty of 05:40 to 08:40 and 13:00 to 19:20 on every day of a 12 days on, 2 days off tour. That is 9 hours 20 minutes of duty across a 13 hour 40 minute spread, against the operator's limits of 10 hours and 14 hours, so the transit fell within 20 minutes of the spread limit. No relief master is rostered. This was unlikely to have influenced the occurrence, because its only path runs through fatigue, which is not established. (Safety issue)
  • The outgoing master told the relieving master at the handover at about 13:05 that the plotter had frozen twice that morning, at 10:42 and 11:17, and neither made an entry in the defect book. This was unlikely to have influenced the occurrence, because an entry at that time could not have led to the firmware fix before 18:07. It matters because both masters described the omission as the usual practice.
  • The forward saloon lifejacket locker holds 40 adult lifejackets behind the kiosk counter and cannot be reached from 22 of the 34 forward saloon seats without passing behind the counter through a 0.6 m gap. The counter was fitted in a 2019 interior refit under a minor modification notice that did not trigger a re-survey. The operator says the same counter is fitted to its two other 24 m vessels. This remains a matter still being examined. It is virtually certain that the locker is blocked in this way. It is unlikely to have influenced the grounding, and it is very likely to be important to address, because the deckhand had to ask three passengers to move and issue the lifejackets over the counter. Whether the arrangement is fleet-wide is [NOT ESTABLISHED: operator's and regulator's answers]. (Safety issue)

Other findings

  • The master stopped both engines 27 seconds after contact and did not attempt to refloat on a falling tide. The vessel was holed in way of the No. 2 starboard void, so the decision avoided putting a flooding vessel into deep water with passengers aboard. This reduced risk.
  • The radio work after the grounding was complete at the first attempt, and all 38 passengers were ashore by 19:26.
  • The shallow alarm and the steering and engine systems worked as designed until the contact.
  • A fall of the tide below prediction was very unlikely. The gauge read 0.03 m below the tide table, and the vessel would have touched at the predicted height as well.
  • A steering or propulsion failure before the vessel left the centreline was very unlikely. The recorder showed steady engine speeds and steering pressure, and every component of the steering system tested serviceable.
  • Whether the unshielded boat ramp floodlights delayed the sighting of the beacon is unresolved, and no conclusion is drawn. It is virtually certain that 14 unshielded floodlights, each presenting about 4,800 candela, lie behind the beacon within 4 degrees of its bearing and 1.5 degrees of its elevation. The master and the outgoing master both described the beacon as lost in the town lighting. The beacon was screened by the canopy for most of the search, and the heading change began before the search. The survey was made eleven days later, nothing establishes a detection threshold for a 0.4 second green flash against that background, and the master said twice that he could not tell whether the lights were the reason. Whether the floodlights contributed is about as likely as not, so the investigation could not settle it on the evidence available.
  • Whether the master was fatigued during the transit is unresolved, and no conclusion is drawn. The master was on day nine of twelve and recorded 6 hours 15 minutes of sleep, and said he was tired. However, the master also said he was not slow, and the helm work, the 4 second response to the alarm and the radio work after the grounding showed no sign of fatigue. No detailed fatigue assessment was made. Fatigue is about as likely as not, so the investigation could not settle it on the evidence available.

What is being done

This section covers each safety issue in turn, the action recorded against it and its current status. Action was recorded against two of the issues, and the rest are listed at the end.

The investigation concluded that the deferral of the beacon's sightline clearing, which was deferred unfunded at three works rounds, very likely contributed to the beacon being screened from the channel. In response, work order WO-176 was funded from the 2026 waterways contingency, and the Merrandi Islet canopy was trimmed to 2 m on 24/07/2026, restoring the No. 4 beacon's sightline over the northern approach. The Harbour Master, Kanooka Heads, reported this action, and it is closed. A three-yearly trimming cycle has been programmed, and the sightline is to be re-measured from the inbound track on completion. The Investigator in charge has also recommended that the aids to navigation services agreement replace the 50 m vegetation scope at schedule 2.4 with a sightline test. This recommendation is open, and a response is due by 30/09/2026.

The conversion of the No. 4 beacon to a solar lantern halved its nominal range, and no notice reached the users of the channel. The investigation found that this did not influence the occurrence, and it remains a risk because the operator's passage plan still described a light of 6 M. The Aids to Navigation Officer, Kanooka Shire Council, issued local notice to waterway users LNM-2026-14 on 22/07/2026. It gave the solar conversion and the 3 M nominal range, and the Port Authority's aids to navigation register was made available to every commercial operator using the channel. Tarrakin Ferries has reissued the Merrandi Channel passage plan appendix as issue 3 with the corrected range. This action is in progress.

The absence of a night passage plan or a hold point for the loss of the primary means of position fixing very likely contributed to the transit continuing at eight knots after the plotter froze. The Investigator in charge has recommended that Tarrakin Ferries write a night passage plan for the Merrandi Channel before any further darkness transit, and that it name a hold point requiring the way to be taken off the vessel when the primary means of position fixing is lost inside the channel, until the position is re-established by another means. This recommendation is open, and a response is due by 30/09/2026.

The investigation recorded no safety action against the other safety issues, namely the following:

  • The defect procedure (OPS-9) did not require a fault that cleared itself to be recorded: [NOT ESTABLISHED: any recorded safety action against the defect procedure (OPS-9) or the unapplied plotter firmware].

- [What happened] - Contact timeline entry (18:12:04) cites "the survey of 08/07/2026", but the survey and slipping report is dated 09/07/2026 to 14/07/2026. - Factor "Unshielded boat ramp floodlights aligned behind the No. 4 beacon from the north" appears as the head of a causal chain to the heading change, yet it is listed as having failed the Influence test. - Factor "Heading eased five degrees to starboard" against the recorded course of 195 degrees at the No. 2 beacon and a held heading of 199 degrees at the channel edge, which is a four-degree difference. This may be a course versus heading distinction, but it should be confirmed. - Critical event evidence describes the furrows as running 11 m "on a heading of 197 degrees", while the timeline records a held heading of 199 degrees. This may also be a track versus heading distinction and is worth confirming. - [Why it happened] - "Unshielded boat ramp floodlights aligned behind the No. 4 beacon from the north": the drafting instruction lists this factor among those that "did not pass the Influence test". The record shows its Influence result as Inconclusive (about as likely as not), not Fail. The text treats it as unresolved and does not place it upstream of the grounding. - "Unshielded boat ramp floodlights aligned behind the No. 4 beacon from the north" is marked Finalised: no, yet it also carries a "Led to: Heading eased five degrees to starboard" link. That link is inconsistent with an Inconclusive Influence result. - "Forward saloon lifejacket locker blocked by a 2019 counter fitted without re-survey" is marked Finalised: no. Its categorisation may still change. - "Master fatigued during the channel transit": the note says whether he "was rostered into that position is tested on the roster object". The roster safety issue failed Influence (unlikely), so that question appears to be closed on the roster object rather than left open. - [What we found] - "Darkness transit rostered to close a split duty within 20 minutes of the spread limit", "Master fatigued during the channel transit" and "Heading eased five degrees to starboard without a decision to turn": the investigator notes date the split or addition to 09/10/2026, but the material was generated on 2026-10-08. The date runs ahead of the generation date. - "Chart plotter display froze during the channel transit and did not recover", "Transit continued at eight knots" and "Shallow alarm at its 2019 setting": the analysis graded the influence of all three as extremely likely. Under the findings-scale rule this has been narrowed to very likely here. The approved "Why it happened" section, however, uses "extremely likely" for these factors, so the two sections now differ in wording. - "No night passage plan or hold point for loss of the primary fix": this factor sits under "Safety issues (organisational level)" and is tagged as a safety issue in this section. The approved "Why it happened" section did not tag it, while it did tag the other three organisational safety issues. - Checklist, Interviews: the item asking whether each interview has been written up, checked against the record and finalised is marked Yes. The deckhand's interview record is marked as not finalised. - [What is being done] - Approved "What we found": the chart plotter freeze and the continued transit at eight knots are each stated as having "very likely" contributed. In the source material both carry Influence "Pass - extremely likely". - Approved "What happened": the held heading is given as 199 degrees. The source material for the heading change and the channel departure gives 200 degrees, and the course over ground came back from 200 to 197 degrees.

  • Investigator notes on "Darkness transit rostered..." and "Master fatigued..." are dated 09/10/2026 ("Split out of the old roster object"). The note on "Heading eased five degrees..." is dated "Added 09/10/2026". All three dates are later than the material's generation date of 2026-10-08.
